extracted.intended_audience: podcast creators and fiction writers adapting podcasts into live shows or novels
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical standards for adapting a fiction podcast (Welcome to Night Vale) into live stage performances and novels, covering storytelling, staging, performer use, audience interaction, and publishing logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your medium
rubrics_metrics.description: “Knowing your medium is so, so, so important.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about the differences between audio-recorded-for-distant-listening and live stage or book formats; make creative choices that serve the particular medium rather than assuming what works in one will work in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and leverage performers' strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on what your performers can do in front of a live audience — e.g., Cecil’s stage training made the live show succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cast and write for the performers’ abilities; allow performers to bring stage skills (timing, physicality, presence) to enhance material beyond a literal reading of script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep or adapt your podcast’s format for live shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Live shows tend to follow the same format as the podcast: crisis news story, community calendar, traffic, fake ads, recurring segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognizable structural elements (news updates, fake ads, recurring segments) to preserve tone and give audiences a familiar framework while adapting content for stage dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for audience presence and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Playing with the audience being there is really important to us as writers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally craft moments that make the audience part of the experience (e.g., scenes that make people talk to each other, look at each other, play a murder-mystery game). Don’t treat the audience as invisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write and direct to allow performers to get off the page
rubrics_metrics.description: “Remember to write and direct in a way that allows your performers to get off the page as much as possible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if performers reference the script, create openness for them to react to audience energy (laughs, silences, tension). Avoid rigid page-bound staging that blocks spontaneous performance choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan narrator arrangement and staging choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you have a single-person narrator, a pair of narrators, or a rapid-fire dialogue troupe — staging follows that choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match narrative delivery to stage concept (single narrator like Night Vale, pair like The Black Tapes, or rapid-fire ensemble like Thrilling Adventure Hour). Having the script onstage is acceptable; staging decisions drive pacing and audience focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shorter, punchier sentences for live performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Long sentences written for a mic in an empty room don’t translate well to stage; 'Shorter, quicker thoughts' work better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite prose/dialogue for oral clarity and immediate address: prioritize brevity, clear beats, and direct audience-facing lines to maintain momentum and comprehension in a live setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simply performing recorded episodes unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking podcast episodes written for the microphone and performing them live can feel 'weirdly flat' because they were written for distant listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting existing episodes, rework structure, pacing, and staging to account for audience presence and live actor dynamics rather than doing a straight reenactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and allow for audience energy (laughs, silence, tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give yourself openness for that energy the audience will give you, whether it’s a laugh or a long silence, whether it’s a tense energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build beats and pauses into the script that can stretch or contract in performance; direct actors to listen and respond rather than mechanically hitting lines at fixed speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have the novel written before submitting to agents/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: “You do have to have your novel written before you submit it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a complete manuscript (or required submission materials) prior to seeking an agent or publisher; do not rely solely on concept or partial drafts when initiating publishing conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether the novel is an extension or a standalone
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: are you writing an extension of your podcast, or telling a whole new story that stands on its own?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether the book depends on podcast familiarity or is accessible to new readers; aim to write work that can 'stand on its own' if you want broader readership beyond existing listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select story focus or character suited to a novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Picking a fan-favorite character (e.g., The Faceless Old Woman) can make a strong candidate to center a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a narrative focus with enough depth and distinct voice to carry long-form fiction; consider characters that intrigue fans and can sustain standalone arcs and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage existing audience interest strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Popularity and fan outreach can 'cue you up' to get an agent and meetings with publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demonstrated audience demand (emails, fan interest) as part of the case when pursuing representation and adaptation opportunities — but still deliver a completed, marketable product.
